meta.reviewer_notes: The passage's pivot is that both parties to a famous quarrel share a premise that the cases do not support, so the distractors are built mostly out of the quarrel the author has stepped away from. The last paragraph does three jobs in quick succession, names two costs, grants the other side a point and then measures the grant, and the two hardest questions are decided there. 2026-10-03 CAT-size pass: 631→507 words, 5→4 paragraphs, 5→4 questions. Dropped p4 after folding its thesis sentence into the close of p3 (its point that the right is no privacy claim repeats p2); tightened p1, p2 and p5; dropped q2 (cannot-be-inferred, an EXCEPT-style question that leaks the passage). Earlier notes that cite the fifth paragraph now mean the last.
meta.tone: cool, redescriptive, unindulgent at the close

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the option about how indexes changed the availability of public records, which is the third paragraph offered as the whole; the passage uses that history as the ground for a redescription and then spends its last two paragraphs pricing the redescription, so a purpose that stops at the history leaves the argument's own work unexplained. Q2's rival is the option about somebody having to judge which enquirers have a reason, which reads like a step too far until the fifth paragraph is checked, where the unevenness of the old friction is stated and the judgement is drawn from it in the next clause. Q3's rival is the option about the neighbour and the stranger, which takes a real observation from the fifth paragraph and adds a designing hand the third paragraph expressly denies by saying nobody designed the expenditure. Q4's rival is the option about so few readers troubling to consult the record, which converts a claim about which enquirers reached it into a claim about how many did. Q5's rival is the option that an unfindable record has effectively ceased to exist, which is the record's defenders speaking and which the passage's final sentence answers by saying such a record stays open to anyone who arrives with a reason. (2026-10-03, CAT-size pass: q2 was dropped, so any note above about it no longer applies.)

paragraphs.text: The right is usually stated as a right of removal. A person who finds that something true about him is being circulated, and who can show that it no longer bears on anything he is now asked to be, may require that it be taken down. The objection is that the record is not his. It belongs to everyone who may one day need to consult it, and a society whose members may edit their own past has agreed to stop having a history. For twenty years the argument has turned only on how much weight each side deserves.

What both parties take for granted is that something is being deleted. In the cases that actually arise, nothing is. The newspaper keeps the report and goes on selling access to it. The court keeps the judgment in the volume it was always in. The register keeps the entry, open to anybody who walks in and asks for it. What changes is narrower and stranger than deletion: whether a machine, given a person's name and nothing else, will hand the item over unasked.

To see why that matters, consider what publicity used to involve. A record could be entirely public and still be, for practical purposes, out of reach. Publicity was a permission and not a delivery. Finding the item meant knowing that it existed and where it was kept, and then spending something to reach it: a train journey, an afternoon of a clerk's time, a year of bound issues turned over by hand. Nobody designed that expenditure and nobody defended it, and it did a job all the same. It rationed retrieval to enquirers who had a reason, because a reason was what made the trouble worth taking. The index removed the rationing without altering a single word of what had been written. So the right is best understood as an attempt to put back, by rule, a friction that used to be supplied by the filing cabinet.

The record's defenders are right about one point: a rule governing retrieval is still a rule about what can be found out, and calling it something other than deletion does not make it free. That is true, and it is a smaller truth than it sounds. A record left standing and unindexed is open to anyone who arrives with a reason to consult it, and closed only to the enquirer who had none. Two consequences follow that the right's supporters welcome less. The first is that it can do nothing for the person whose complaint is that the report was false; that is a claim about content, and needs a remedy aimed at the record. The second is that the old friction was never evenly spread: it was slight for a neighbour and heavy for a stranger, so putting it back by rule requires somebody to decide, name by name, which enquirers count as neighbours. The right thus calls for the very judgement about who deserves to know a thing that it was supposed to save people from.

questions.target_mistake: naming the history of retrieval in the third paragraph as the purpose, when that history is the ground for a redescription the last paragraph then prices
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to name a verb and an object: recast a disputed right as a rule about what a machine offers unasked, and then say what the recasting costs.
questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is

options.A: to redescribe a disputed right as a rule about retrieval rather than deletion, and to say what that costs
options.B: to warn that a society whose members may edit their own past will be left with no history, and to name the archives most at risk
options.C: to explain how indexes changed the availability of public records, and to say how far that change can be undone
options.D: to trace how a technology can dissolve a social arrangement that no institution had deliberately established

explanation.expert_notice: The second paragraph names the shared premise and refuses it in two sentences: both parties take deletion for granted, and in the cases that arise nothing is deleted. The third paragraph ends by stating what the right is instead, and the last spends its length on what that account costs its own supporters.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option carries both movements. The redescription is the move from deletion to retrieval, argued for by the newspaper that keeps its report and the register that keeps its entry; the costs are the two consequences the last paragraph names, that nothing is offered to the person whose report was false and that somebody must now judge which enquirers count. A purpose that stops at the redescription leaves the last paragraph with no work to do.
explanation.question_type_note: Primary purpose is a verb with an object, and in a passage that replaces one account with another the limits of the replacement belong inside the purpose, not outside it.
explanation.reading_habit: Count the paragraphs a candidate purpose accounts for. If the closing movement is left over, the candidate has named a stage of the argument rather than its point.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the objection as the first paragraph states it, in order to show that it shares a premise with the right it attacks, and the author holds that the record survives intact. No archive is named or ranked anywhere either, since the second paragraph has the newspaper, the court and the register all keeping exactly what they had.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the most quotable sentence in the opening and it is not labelled as somebody else's, so a reader who fixes the purpose early carries a stated objection away as a stated warning.

distractors.why_wrong: The history of retrieval is used as the ground for the redescription that closes its paragraph, and how far the change could be undone is never asked. Offered as the purpose it makes the last paragraph, where the author prices his own account, look like an appendix.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the material is concrete, it is true of the passage, and it is the part a reader is most likely to remember when asked what the passage was about.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage is about what one disputed right actually is and what the redescription costs, not about technologies and arrangements in general. The friction really is described as something nobody designed, and that observation is used to explain a single remedy rather than to trace any wider process.
distractors.seductive_element: It is abstract, it sounds like the sort of thing an essay of this kind ought to be doing, and it borrows the passage's most interesting observation in order to do it.

questions.target_mistake: taking the unevenness described in the last paragraph as something the old arrangement was designed to produce
questions.stem: According to the passage, before indexes existed a record that was entirely public could still be

options.A: withheld by the office that kept it from an enquirer unable to give a reason for asking
options.B: corrected at the request of the person concerned, provided the entry could be shown to be wrong
options.C: out of reach in practice, since reaching it cost an effort few would take without a reason
options.D: consulted easily by a neighbour and only with difficulty by a stranger, an unevenness the law had arranged

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph states it in consecutive sentences. A record could be entirely public and still be out of reach; publicity was a permission and not a delivery; finding the item cost a journey, a clerk's afternoon, a year of issues turned by hand. The paragraph then names the effect of that cost, which was to ration retrieval to enquirers who had a reason.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is those sentences compressed. The point is not that anyone refused an enquirer but that the record sat behind an expense, and the expense was paid only by people with a motive for paying it. That is what makes the whole argument possible, since the index is then described as having removed a rationing device without removing anything from the record.
explanation.question_type_note: A detail question about a past arrangement turns on what the passage says the arrangement did, not on what somebody might have intended by it. Put a finger on the sentence.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage says an arrangement did a job that nobody designed, keep the two apart in your notes. Half the distractors in such sets restore the designer the author removed.

distractors.why_wrong: No office refuses anybody in this passage. The register is described as staying open to whoever walks in and asks, and the barrier the third paragraph names is the cost of reaching the item rather than a decision by its keeper.
distractors.seductive_element: The paragraph does say retrieval was rationed to enquirers with a reason, and rationing sounds like something a person administers.

distractors.why_wrong: Correction belongs to the last paragraph, where it is named as a different claim needing a different remedy. Nothing is said about whether it was available before indexes existed, and the stem asks about what a public record could be.
distractors.seductive_element: Correcting a wrong entry is the reform a reader most expects in this area, and the passage mentions falsity often enough to keep it in mind.

distractors.why_wrong: The unevenness is real and is stated in the last paragraph, and the arranging hand is not. The third paragraph says in terms that nobody designed the expenditure and nobody defended it, and that it did its job all the same.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because both halves use the passage's own material and the second half supplies the tidy explanation a reader expects an argument about law to be heading towards.

questions.target_mistake: reading the concrete examples as a measure of how slow retrieval used to be, rather than as a demonstration of what the slowness accomplished
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: the examples are there to show what the cost of finding a record used to do, before anybody had to decide it.
questions.stem: The author mentions the train journey and the year of bound issues chiefly in order to

options.A: illustrate how much faster an old record can be reached now than it could be then
options.B: suggest that newspaper archives were badly kept before anyone thought to index them
options.C: explain why so few readers, however open the record, ever troubled to consult it
options.D: show that the effort of finding a record once did, with nobody deciding it, the rationing now done by rule

explanation.expert_notice: The examples arrive in the middle of a paragraph whose next sentences say what they are for. Nobody designed the expenditure; it did a job all the same; it rationed retrieval to enquirers who had a reason. The paragraph then closes by naming the right as an attempt to put that same rationing back by rule.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option names the job. A detail earns its place by what it does for the claim around it, and this one supplies the thing the author's redescription needs: a rationing device that existed, worked, and belonged to nobody. Without it the closing talk of restoring a friction would have nothing to restore.
explanation.question_type_note: A why-does-the-author-mention question is answered by the claim the detail serves, which is almost always stated within a sentence or two of the detail itself.
explanation.reading_habit: When you meet a vivid concrete list in an abstract passage, read on to the next claim before deciding what the list is for. Authors put examples in front of the sentence they are buying.

distractors.why_wrong: The contrast in speed is real and it is not what the examples are doing. The paragraph does not treat the old slowness as an inconvenience that has since been cured; it treats it as a filter whose removal is the whole subject of the passage.
distractors.seductive_element: Then and now comparisons are what concrete details usually carry, and the speed of retrieval is the first difference any reader notices.

distractors.why_wrong: Nothing is said about how well or badly any archive was kept. The difficulty described belongs to the enquirer's journey and the enquirer's afternoon, not to the order of anybody's shelves.
distractors.seductive_element: Bound issues turned over by hand sound like a complaint about organisation, and readers convert descriptions of inconvenience into criticisms of the people responsible.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph says which enquirers reached the record, not how many. Its claim is that the cost selected for people with a reason, which is compatible with a great many such people and says nothing about the size of the readership.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because a cost that few would pay does reduce numbers, and the step from selection to scarcity is small enough to make without noticing.

questions.target_mistake: treating a record that is hard to find as a record that has been destroyed, which is the premise the passage removes in its second paragraph
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the difference will be about what each request asks to have changed: whether the item is offered, or what the item says.
questions.stem: It can be inferred that a request to remove a name from an index differs from a request to correct a false report in that

options.A: the first is a matter for the courts and the second for the publication that made the error
options.B: the first grows stronger as the record ages and the second is as strong on the day of publication
options.C: the first is the graver of the two, since a record that nobody can find, though still on the shelf, has ceased to exist
options.D: the first leaves the record intact and asks only that it stop being offered unasked

explanation.expert_notice: Two sentences do the work and they sit in different paragraphs. The second says what actually changes: whether a machine given a name will hand the item over unasked. The last says what the right cannot reach: a complaint that the report was false, which is a claim about content and needs a remedy aimed at the record.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option puts those together as a difference. One request concerns the offering of an item and leaves every word of it in place; the other concerns the words themselves and cannot be satisfied by any rule about offering. That is why the author says the right can do nothing for the person whose report was wrong, and the inference is one step rather than three.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference question about a difference is answered by finding where each of the two things is described and comparing the descriptions, not by supplying a difference that sounds likely.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author says a remedy cannot reach a certain complaint, ask what the remedy does reach. The contrast is usually the cleanest inference the passage will support.

distractors.why_wrong: No forum is assigned to either request anywhere in the passage. Courts appear once, as keepers of judgments, and the argument is about what each request asks to be changed rather than about who is to hear it.
distractors.seductive_element: Legal disputes come with venues, and a reader who has slipped into thinking about procedure will find this the most practical looking option on offer.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage makes neither claim stronger or weaker with time. Its one temporal remark is the requester's showing that the item no longer bears on what he is now asked to be, which is a condition on bringing the request, not a growth in its force.
distractors.seductive_element: The idea that old information deserves to be let go is the intuition most readers bring to this subject, and the passage's first sentences invite it.

distractors.why_wrong: The last paragraph says the reverse just after granting the record's defenders their point: a record left standing and unindexed is open to anyone who arrives with a reason, and closed only to the enquirer who had none.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because it is the record's defenders speaking in their strongest form, and the passage takes their case seriously enough that a reader may take this for the conclusion.

vocabulary.meaning_here: the condition of being open to public inspection

vocabulary.passage_use: It rationed retrieval to enquirers who had a reason
vocabulary.meaning_here: limited access to a share of those who qualified for it

a system that returns items in answer to a name

mentor.challenge: Two famous positions are set against each other and then both are told they were arguing about the wrong thing. Watch what the author says actually changes in these cases, because half the questions here are decided by that one sentence.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: The quarrel between a right of removal and the value of the record assumes that something is deleted, whereas in the cases that arise the newspaper, the court and the register all keep what they had and only the machine's willingness to offer it changes, so the right is best read as an attempt to restore by rule the friction that finding a record used to cost, which means it cannot help the person whose record was false and obliges somebody to decide, name by name, which enquirers are to be treated as neighbours.
mentor.main_idea: A right to have information about oneself removed is usually defended as a matter of dignity and attacked as an attack on the historical record. Both sides assume deletion. In practice nothing is deleted: the archives keep everything, and what changes is whether a search on a person's name offers the item unasked. Read that way, the right is an attempt to put back the effort that finding a record used to cost, since that effort quietly rationed retrieval to people who had a reason. The account narrows the right sharply and gives it two costs its friends dislike.
mentor.simple_explanation:
There is a long argument about whether a person should be able to have old information about himself taken down. One side says yes: it is true but out of date, and it no longer has anything to do with who he is now. The other side says no: the record belongs to everybody, and a society where people edit their own past has given up on having a history.

The author's first move is to say that both sides are describing something that is not happening. Look at the actual cases. The newspaper still has the article and still sells it. The court still has the judgment in the same book. The office still has the entry, and anyone can walk in and ask for it. Nothing has been destroyed. The only thing that changes is whether a machine, when you type a person's name and nothing else, hands you the item without being asked for it.

Then he explains why that is such a big difference. Think about what being public used to mean. A record could be completely public and still be almost impossible to get at. You had to know it existed, know where it was, and then spend something to reach it: a train journey, an afternoon of a clerk's time, a whole year of newspapers turned over page by page. Nobody planned that and nobody defended it, but it did something useful. It meant that the only people who actually found the record were people who had a reason to look. The search index took that filter away without changing a single word on any page. So the right is really an attempt to put that filter back on purpose, by making a rule, because the filing cabinet is no longer doing it for free.

He grants the other side a point: a rule about what can be found is still a rule about what people can learn, and calling it something other than deletion does not make it costless. But the point is smaller than it looks, because a record that is still on the shelf and simply not indexed is open to anyone who turns up with a reason. Then come two costs that the right's supporters enjoy less. First, it gives nothing to the person whose real complaint is that the story about him was untrue; that needs a remedy aimed at what the record says. Second, the old filter was never fair. It was easy for a neighbour and hard for a stranger. So putting it back by rule means somebody has to decide, case by case, which enquirers count as neighbours, which is exactly the kind of judgement about who deserves to know things that the right was supposed to spare people.
mentor.why_difficult: The passage refuses a premise that both familiar positions share, so a reader who arrives with either side's vocabulary keeps supplying deletion where the author has put retrieval, and several of the distractors are built from exactly that substitution. The second difficulty is the third paragraph, which describes an arrangement that worked and insists nobody designed it; readers restore the designer, because a filter that selects enquirers feels like something somebody must have decided. The third is the last paragraph, which grants the opposing side a point, measures the grant, and then names two costs, all in the space a hurried reader has already begun to skim.
mentor.author_intention: To take a stale quarrel away from both parties by showing that the case they are arguing about does not occur, and then to make the reader pay for the clearer description by facing the two things it rules out.

paragraph_journey.note: A right to have old information taken down, and the objection that the record belongs to everybody. Both are given in their strongest form.
Nothing is deleted in real cases. The archives keep everything. What changes is whether a machine offers the item when you type a name.
Being public used to be a permission, not a delivery. The trouble of finding a record quietly limited it to people with a reason to look, and the right tries to put that friction back by rule.

paragraph_journey.role: Prices it, and measures the grant
paragraph_journey.note: The other side is granted a point and it is immediately cut down to size. Then the two costs: nothing for a false report, and somebody must now judge which enquirers count.

mentor.tone_progression: It opens even-handed, almost weary with a familiar quarrel, becomes brisk and factual as the cases are described, warms slightly in the history of the filing cabinet, and ends cool and unindulgent, naming two costs and refusing to let a concession grow larger than the sentence it was made in.
key_transitions: 'What both parties take for granted is that something is being deleted.' (opening of paragraph 2): the shared premise is named and removed.
'So the right is best understood as an attempt to put back, by rule, a friction that used to be supplied by the filing cabinet.' (close of paragraph 3): the replacement account arrives.
'That is true, and it is a smaller truth than it sounds.' (paragraph 4): a point granted to the other side is immediately measured.
mentor.misunderstanding: The commonest wrong model is that the author is on the side of the right and has found a clever way of saying that nothing is really lost. He is not: he says a rule about retrieval is still a rule about what can be found out, and he loads two costs onto the account he prefers. The opposite wrong model reads the last paragraph's concession as the conclusion and comes away thinking an unindexed record has effectively been destroyed, which the paragraph denies at once by saying such a record remains open to anyone with a reason to consult it.
mentor.traps_summary: This set offers the history of retrieval as the purpose, a real unevenness with an invented designer behind it, a claim about how many readers consulted a record in place of a claim about which ones did, and the opposing side's strongest sentence as the author's conclusion. Sorting each option into quarrel, refusal, history, replacement or price answers all four.
mentor.reading_lesson: When an author says that two opposed positions share a premise, stop arguing between them and find the sentence where the premise is replaced, because everything the passage does afterwards is built on the replacement and every distractor will be built on the premise. The companion habit is to watch what an author does immediately after granting an opponent a point: a concession followed by a measuring sentence is a concession that has been priced, and reading only the first half of that pair is the most common way to lose a passage in its final paragraph.
mentor.real_world: The same distinction runs through any argument about what a system may show rather than what it may hold: a criminal record that stays on file but drops off an employer's standard check, a disciplinary finding that survives in a regulator's archive without appearing beside a practitioner's name, a school report kept but not forwarded. In each, the fight that looks like a fight about deletion is a fight about who gets offered the item without asking.
mentor.takeaway: A record nobody deletes and nobody offers is not private; it is simply back to costing something to find.
mentor.reflection_question: Which things that are true about you were protected for years by nothing more than the trouble of looking them up?

eli10.big_idea: Nothing is really deleted: the right only stops searches offering old facts unasked, and that has costs.
eli10.story: Some say old but true news about you should be taken down. Others say the record belongs to everyone. The writer says both sides are arguing about the wrong thing. Nothing is deleted. The newspaper and the court keep everything. What changes is whether a search hands it over when someone types your name. Long ago, reaching a public record took a train trip or days with old newspapers. Nobody planned this, but it worked like a filter. Only people with a real reason took the trouble. It was like a book in a faraway library: open to all, but only keen readers made the trip. The right tries to rebuild that filter by rule. He admits that still limits learning, but anyone with a reason can look. It has two costs. It does nothing if the story was false. And someone must judge whose reason is good enough.
paragraphs: Sets out the quarrel: a right to have true old facts taken down, against the record belonging to everyone.
Says both sides miss one thing: nothing is deleted; only what a search offers changes.
Explains with history: effort once filtered who looked, and the right tries to restore that by rule.
Grants a point, then names two costs: no help for false stories, and someone must judge who counts.
eli10.author_view: The writer is cool and fair: he clears up a muddled quarrel, then makes the right's supporters face its costs.
